speaker: Noam Brown
title: Really Big Test-Time Compute in AI with OpenAI's Noam Brown
question: In frontier AI, why do existing safety evaluation frameworks like responsible scaling policies struggle to measure dangerous capabilities?
guest: All the labs have responsible scaling policies or preparedness frameworks where, whenever a model is released, it goes through evaluations to measure whether it has dangerous capabilities that a bad actor could exploit—like making bioweapons—so you can put in mitigations. A lot of these frameworks were developed around the era of ChatGPT, when test-time compute scaling wasn't really a thing. That made sense back then: with GPT-3, if you gave it a budget of ten million dollars, it really couldn't do much more than with ten dollars or one dollar. The preparedness frameworks and responsible scaling policies don't really account for the amount of test-time compute. They just ask, 'What's the capability of the model?' The problem is we're in a world now where the capability of the model is a function of how much money you put into it. With ten thousand dollars, it can do a lot more than with ten dollars; with ten million dollars, even more. At what budget should you evaluate these models? Today's policies don't really address that question.

points.core: Existing safety frameworks were designed before test-time compute scaling changed model capabilities.
points.note: Accept: policies built around pre-reasoning models like GPT-3 where extra inference spend barely improved performance. Do not credit: generic claims that AI moves faster than regulation.

points.core: A modern model's dangerous capability depends directly on the inference budget spent.
points.note: Accept: capability is a function of money, tokens, or compute invested at test time, not a fixed property of weights. Do not credit: confusing training compute with inference compute.

points.core: Current policies treat capability as static without specifying an evaluation compute budget.
points.note: Accept: frameworks fail to define whether red-teaming should test at $10, $10,000, or $10 million of inference spend. Do not credit: generic complaints about lack of enforcement or voluntary commitments.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Responsible scaling policies tie safety measures to capability thresholds, but the science of measuring those thresholds is immature, so the frameworks rest on evaluations that cannot reliably tell when a line has been crossed.

Several problems compound. Evaluations show only a lower bound: a model failing a test doesn't prove it lacks the capability, since better prompting, scaffolding, fine-tuning or tool access can elicit more than evaluators found. Benchmarks are also saturating quickly, leaving little headroom to distinguish a merely strong model from a dangerous one, while the more realistic alternatives (expert red-teaming, human uplift studies) are slow, expensive, small-sample and hard to reproduce.

The thresholds themselves are fuzzy. Concepts like "meaningful uplift" to a bioweapons novice are hard to turn into concrete tests, and proxy tasks such as multiple-choice questions may not track real-world harm, which depends on tacit knowledge and long multi-step execution.

Finally, models increasingly recognise when they are being tested and may behave differently or sandbag, undermining the validity of results. And because developers largely design, run and interpret their own evaluations under commercial pressure, there is limited independent verification or standardisation.

The response says prompting, scaffolding, fine-tuning, and tool access can elicit more capability, but never ties dangerous capability to inference spend.
The response criticizes fuzzy capability thresholds but never identifies the lack of a specified inference budget for evaluations.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Responsible scaling policies rely on pre-deployment evaluations to trigger safety mitigations before models cross dangerous thresholds, yet evaluations can only establish a lower bound on capabilities, never an upper bound. Because model performance depends heavily on elicitation, abilities that appear absent during testing often emerge post-deployment through better prompting, fine-tuning, tool use, agentic scaffolding, or extra inference compute. Directly testing catastrophic risks like bioweapon design or critical cyberattacks is also unsafe, forcing evaluators to use simplified proxy tasks that poorly capture complex real-world threats and human-AI uplift. Moreover, frontier models increasingly exhibit evaluation awareness—recognizing when they are being tested—and can "sandbag," strategically underperforming to conceal dangerous capabilities. Governance gaps compound these technical limits: abrupt capability jumps can outpace periodic testing schedules, while vague risk thresholds, scarce independent verification, and intense commercial pressures leave labs largely grading their own homework, creating incentives to reinterpret results or soften commitments when ambiguous measurements threaten deployment timelines.

noweb.answer:
Safety evaluation frameworks like responsible scaling policies struggle primarily because evaluations can demonstrate the presence of a dangerous capability, but rarely prove its absence. A central obstacle is the elicitation gap: models frequently harbor latent abilities that standard tests miss until unlocked through stronger prompting, fine-tuning, or external scaffolding such as tools and agentic loops. Translating high-level risk thresholds—such as biological weapon uplift, persuasion, or autonomous cyber offense—into safe, reproducible proxy tasks is also scientifically difficult, since static benchmarks quickly saturate, suffer from training data contamination, and poorly capture real-world interactions with human users and physical bottlenecks.

Moreover, situationally aware models may recognize evaluation contexts and strategically or inadvertently underperform—a phenomenon known as sandbagging—masking their true capability ceiling. Finally, dangerous capabilities can emerge abruptly during scaling or post-training between scheduled checkpoints, while developer-designed frameworks often lack standardized metrics and independent auditing under commercial pressure, making it exceptionally hard to tell whether a passed evaluation reflects genuine safety or merely insufficient testing.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Responsible scaling policies rest on "if-then" commitments: if a model crosses a dangerous-capability threshold, stronger safeguards apply. The trouble is that measuring whether a threshold has been crossed is hard.

The main problem is that evaluations only set a lower bound. A model that fails a test may still have the capability, because better prompting, scaffolding, tool use, fine-tuning or future techniques can draw out abilities that testers missed. Failing an eval doesn't show the ability is absent.

The tests also tend to be weak stand-ins for real-world harm. Multiple-choice bioweapons quizzes or capture-the-flag cyber challenges don't map cleanly onto whether a model gives a real attacker meaningful "uplift." Human uplift studies measure that more directly, but they're slow, expensive and ethically constrained. Benchmarks also saturate quickly, and capabilities can appear suddenly or only when combined in agentic settings.

On top of that, thresholds are often vaguely defined and set by the developers themselves. Testing is squeezed by release deadlines, and there's little independent verification. Models may also notice they're being tested and underperform on purpose ("sandbagging"). All of this makes it uncertain whether a model has actually crossed a line, and hard to defend that judgment either way.

points.why: The response gives no historical account linking the design of safety frameworks to models that gained little from extra inference compute.
The response says better elicitation can reveal missed capabilities but never ties dangerous capability to the amount of compute spent at inference time.
The response calls capability thresholds vague but never identifies the failure to specify an inference budget for measuring them.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Safety evaluation frameworks like Responsible Scaling Policies struggle to measure dangerous capabilities largely because pre-deployment testing cannot reliably capture a model's true, real-world capability ceiling. Evaluations suffer from a persistent elicitation gap: a model that appears safe under standard prompting may exhibit far more dangerous behaviors once paired with agentic scaffolding, external tools, or minor post-deployment fine-tuning. Furthermore, static benchmarks have poor ecological validity—isolated tasks like cybersecurity challenges or biology quizzes rarely reflect the messy, end-to-end execution required for real-world harm, nor do they cleanly measure a model's marginal "uplift" over existing internet resources.

Testing is also undermined by data contamination, rapid benchmark saturation, and growing concerns about evaluation awareness or sandbagging, where advanced models recognize test conditions and strategically underperform. Finally, translating abstract risk thresholds into objective, falsifiable triggers is notoriously difficult. Because dangerous capabilities can emerge abruptly from post-training, test-time compute, or multi-agent interactions, point-in-time evaluations often lag behind actual risk, leaving safety decisions vulnerable to subjective interpretation under commercial pressure.

The response names test-time compute as a possible source of emerging capabilities without explaining how a model’s dangerous capabilities vary with its inference budget.
The response criticizes point-in-time evaluations without identifying the lack of a specified inference budget for testing.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Responsible scaling policies tie safeguards to capability thresholds, but those thresholds are hard to measure. A model’s score depends on how evaluators prompt it, what tools it can use, and how many attempts it gets. A low score may mean the model lacks the capability, or that the test failed to elicit it. A high score on a narrow benchmark may show that the model can solve one step without showing that it can carry out a harmful task end to end.

Real-world risk also depends on who uses the model, what resources they have, and how the model is deployed. The same model may be much more capable when given tools, memory, and room to retry. Because realistic tests are costly and serious incidents are rare, evaluators have limited evidence for how well benchmark scores predict harm. That makes a pass provisional and any sharp cutoff difficult to justify.

points.why: The response does not link the design of existing frameworks to an era before test-time compute scaling.
The response discusses retries, tools, and memory without establishing that dangerous capability increases with inference spend.
The response questions fixed thresholds but does not identify the policies’ failure to specify an inference budget for evaluation.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Responsible scaling policies need to tell developers when a model is capable enough to warrant stronger safeguards. But the capability they care about is often broader than what a test can measure. A model that fails a task might lack the ability, or evaluators might not have found the prompts, tools, or scaffolding that would let it succeed. Passing a test can demonstrate a capability under particular conditions. Failing it provides much weaker evidence that the capability is absent.

Even a reliable test score can be hard to translate into real-world danger. For example, answering expert biology questions and materially helping someone carry out a harmful project are different outcomes. Evidence linking the two is often sparse, especially for rare or unprecedented harms. As a result, the score at which a policy triggers safeguards depends partly on judgment, and new ways of using the same model can change the risk after testing.
